extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners as secondary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description, enablement, best mode, and definiteness) including when to make rejections and which form paragraphs to use. Focuses on how to determine invention, assess disclosure adequacy, and identify missing or essential subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what the invention is
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention is defined in the claims. The specification need not set forth details not relating to the essence of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify the invention by the claims. Unclaimed matter unrelated to the operation of the claimed invention does not trigger requirements (cites: In re Bosy; Northern Telecom v. Samsung; Eli Lilly & Co. v. Barr Labs). Focus examination on claim-defined invention; do not require disclosure of irrelevant details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific example is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statutory requirement for disclosure of a specific example; the absence (or presence) of a working example is not dispositive of best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent specifications are not production specifications (cites: In re Gay). Best mode may be represented by a preferred range of conditions or group of reactants (In re Honn). Do not treat lack of a concrete example alone as evidence of failure to disclose best mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation as best mode is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors are not required to point out which embodiment they consider their best; inclusion of the best mode in the disclosure suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement labeling an embodiment as the 'best' is unnecessary to satisfy the statute (cites: Ernsthausen v. Nakayama). Examiners should not demand explicit designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating best mode is not required for priority claims
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement to update the best mode in foreign priority or earlier-filed benefit claims; the earlier-filed disclosure governs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119, 119(e), or 120, the disclosure in the earlier-filed application must satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA first paragraph 'other than the requirement to disclose the best mode.' See Standard Oil Co. v. Montedison. Consult MPEP § 2165 II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect in best mode cannot be cured by new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If the best mode contemplated at filing is not disclosed, the defect cannot be cured by adding the missing best mode later as new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments that add a specific mode not described in the application as filed should be treated as new matter and objected to (cites: In re Hay). Such amendments implicate 35 U.S.C. 132 and 251 and should be coupled with cancellation of the new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement distinct from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The best mode requirement is a separate and distinct requirement from the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate lack of any mode (nonenablement) with best mode. Best mode addresses whether inventor knew of a preferred mode and failed to disclose it, while enablement addresses whether the disclosure places the claimed subject matter generally in the public's possession (cites: In re Newton; In re Glass).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to disclose specific instrumentalities recognized as best
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant develops specific instrumentalities or techniques recognized at filing as the best way to carry out the invention, the best mode provision imposes an obligation to disclose that information to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventor has developed particular techniques or instrumentalities not generally known and recognized as best, the disclosure must include them (cites: Spectra-Physics v. Coherent). Assess whether inventor had such specific information at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume best mode is disclosed unless evidence to the contrary
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should assume the best mode is disclosed in the application unless presented with evidence inconsistent with that assumption; best mode rejections are extremely rare in ex parte prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because relevant evidence about an inventor's state of mind is often inaccessible to examiners, a best mode rejection should normally not be made absent clear evidence to the contrary. Consult supervisors if earlier-filed applications are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part best mode analysis (subjective + objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper best mode analysis has two components: (A) whether, at filing, the inventor knew of a mode he considered better than any other (subjective); and (B) if so, whether the disclosure is adequate to enable one skilled in the art to practice that best mode (objective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only if component (A) is satisfied (inventor knew of a preferred mode) should the examiner analyze (B). A best mode rejection is proper only if (A) can be answered affirmatively and (B) negatively with reasons showing the specification is nonenabling for the best mode (cites: Chemcast v. Arco). The adequacy assessment depends on the level of skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider only evidence of concealment when assessing best mode adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing whether the best mode disclosure is adequate, only evidence that tends to show concealment (intentional or accidental) should be considered; the evidence must show the disclosure quality effectively amounts to concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for indications that the disclosure is so poor it conceals the best mode. Examples of acceptable disclosures (not concealment) include cases where routine skill suffices to produce workable program, known substitutes widely available, known methods that SKA would use, or where disclosed procedures correspond to those actually used (cites: In re Sherwood; Honeywell v. Diamond; W.L. Gore; High Concrete; Scripps Clinic; Amgen). Examples of concealment include failure to disclose non-obvious preferred processing details contrary to literature (Spectra-Physics) or omission of necessary surface treatment known to inventor (Dana Corp. v. IPC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using it in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the same; it shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.30.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis) where required (first actions on the merits and final rejections). Rejections under written description (form paragraph 7.31.01) must identify subject matter not described in the application as filed and explain why possession of the claimed invention at filing is in doubt. Precede such rejections with 7.30.01 or 7.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for lack of written description (form paragraph 7.31.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA first paragraph) as failing to comply with the written description requirement because claim contains subject matter not described so as to reasonably convey possession to one skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. In the bracketed explanation, identify (by page/line or figures) the subject matter not described and explain the position, including unresolved examiner questions that raise doubt as to possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (form paragraph 7.31.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as failing to comply with the enablement requirement because the claim contains subject matter not described in a way to enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. If problem is scope (breadth vs disclosure), consider form paragraph 7.31.03. In explanations, identify claimed subject matter for which the specification is not enabling and explain why using the In re Wands factors as appropriate (see MPEP §§ 2164.01(a), 2164.04). Include examiner questions not resolved that raise doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of enablement must be commensurate with claim scope (form paragraph 7.31.03)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject when the specification, while enabling for some subject matter, does not reasonably provide enablement commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 7.31.03 when some embodiments are enabled but the claims are broader than the enabling disclosure. Identify what is enabling (bracket 2), aspects of claims not enabled (bracket 3), and whether the claim fails to enable to 'make,' 'use,' or 'make and use' (bracket 4). Explain with In re Wands factors and cite specific portions of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode rejection (form paragraph 7.31.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA) first paragraph because the best mode contemplated has not been disclosed; evidence of concealment is based upon [2].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. In bracket 2, insert the basis for holding best mode concealed (e.g., disclosure quality so poor as to effectively result in concealment). Use rarely; follow MPEP §§ 2165–2165.04 for when such rejections are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement of 'single means' / means-plus-function claims (form paragraph 7.31.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected because it purports to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph) but fails to recite a combination of elements as required, reciting instead a function with no limits while the specification discloses at most the means known to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph is to be used only when a claim recites a single element in means-plus-function format. Such rejection is rare. Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. Explain how the claim recites a function without limits and why the disclosure is not commensurate with the broad functional claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential subject matter missing from claims (form paragraph 7.33.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA) first paragraph as based on a disclosure which is not enabling because the disclosure does not enable one of ordinary skill in the art to practice the invention without [2], which is critical or essential but not included in the claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. In bracket 2, recite the omitted subject matter. Provide the rationale for considering it critical or essential (bracket 3) and cite statements, arguments, dates, drawings, or other evidence demonstrating the applicant considered the feature essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two separate requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) Claims must set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention (subjective). (B) Claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter to be protected (objective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as separate inquiries: (A) depends on inventor's perspective (evidence outside the specification may show divergence); (B) is an objective definiteness requirement evaluated against a hypothetical person of ordinary skill. Rejections under 112(b) should identify whether the basis is indefiniteness or failure to claim what inventor regards as invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for failure to claim subject matter inventor regards as invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on failure of the claims to set forth subject matter inventor regards as the invention is appropriate only where inventor has stated elsewhere (outside the application as filed) that the invention is different from what is defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence 'to the contrary' may come from applicant remarks, briefs, or 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits (cites: Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark; In re Prater; In re Cormany). Do not use the specification content as evidence for this inquiry; see MPEP § 2172 for guidance and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed essential subject matter: multiple possible rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitted matter that appears necessary to describe or make the invention may justify rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement or written description) or under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness or failure to claim what inventor regards as invention), depending on facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP § 2163 and § 2164 guidance to determine whether to make a written description/enablement rejection. If claim fails to interrelate essential elements, consider indefiniteness under 112(b). Provide reasons and cite appropriate case law (e.g., In re Mayhew; Gentry Gallery; In re Venezia) and explain why omitted matter is critical or essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (definiteness requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be definite so the scope is clear to persons skilled in the art; if not, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) as indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefiniteness rejections must clearly identify the language causing indefiniteness and thoroughly explain the reasoning. The primary purpose is clear public notice of claim boundaries; secondary purpose is to permit assessment of compliance with other patentability criteria. Require applicant response to explain or amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting claims — applicants are their own lexicographers
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may define terms in their specification; claim language may be functional, use alternative expressions, negative limitations, or any style so long as any special meaning assigned is clearly set forth in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject a claim solely because of the type of language used. Allow applicant-defined meanings if clear in the specification (see MPEP § 2111.01, In re Swinehart). Apply the claim interpretation principles (e.g., broadest reasonable interpretation for FITF applications) when evaluating definiteness and claim scope.
